question: The café worker asks, “Are you eating in?” What does she want to know?
choices: Do you want a bigger meal?
Will you eat your food here?
Would you like to see the menu?
Have you had lunch already?
note: “Eat in” means stay in the café for your meal. If you’re leaving with your food, ask for it “to take away”.

question: You ask for your salad dressing “on the side”. Where do you want it?
choices: In a separate little dish.
Under the salad leaves.
On top of all the salad.
On a different table.
note: With the dressing on the side, you can put as much as you like on your salad.

picture.alt: A bowl of salad with croutons.

question: You order a drink. The café worker asks, “Anything else?” What is she asking?
choices: Would you like a different drink instead?
Did you order this yesterday?
Would you like the drink later?
Would you like to order more?
note: “Anything else?” asks if your order is complete. “That’s all, thanks” means you’ve finished ordering.

question: You ask for a cheese sandwich. The café worker says, “Sorry, we’re out of cheese.” What does she mean?
choices: The cheese costs extra.
The cheese is outside.
There’s no cheese left.
The cheese is in the sandwich.
note: If a café is out of something, it can’t serve it now. It might have some again tomorrow.

question: At the end of lunch someone says, “Could we have the bill, please?” What do they want?
choices: To ask for some more food.
To see how much they must pay.
To see where they can sit.
To book a table for later.
note: The bill shows the food and drinks you’re paying for. A receipt shows you have paid.

question: You arrive at a café with two friends. The waiter asks, “How many of you are there?” What do you say?
choices: A table for three, please.
Three coffees, please.
There are two of my friends here.
Could we sit by the window, please?
note: “Two of my friends” counts your friends. The waiter needs three seats because you’re eating too.

question: You like the cheese and tomato sandwich on the menu, but don’t like tomatoes. You still want the cheese. What do you ask?
choices: Could I have something else instead?
Could I have the tomatoes on the side?
Could you recommend a different sandwich?
Could I have that without tomato?
note: “On the side” keeps tomatoes on your plate in a separate place. “Without tomato” asks the kitchen to leave them out.

picture.alt: A triangular sandwich with cheese and cucumber between slices of bread.

question: You order coffee. “Hot or iced?” asks the worker. It’s cold outside and you want to warm your hands on the cup. What do you say?
choices: A black coffee, please.
A small one, please.
Hot, please.
Which one do you recommend?
note: “Black” tells the worker you take it without milk. It could still be hot or iced, so “Hot, please” answers the question.

question: Your tea arrives, but your sandwich doesn’t. Ten minutes pass. You want to check on the sandwich you ordered. What do you say?
choices: Can I order another sandwich, please?
Excuse me, is my sandwich coming?
Could I have the bill, please?
Could I order a sandwich, please?
note: “Another sandwich” could bring a second one. “Is my sandwich coming?” checks the order you’ve already made.

question: You and a friend shared some biscuits. One biscuit is left. You’d like your friend to have it. What do you say?
choices: Would you like the last one?
Could I have the last one?
Shall we share the last one?
Was that the last one?
note: Sharing gives you half each. “Would you like the last one?” offers your friend the whole biscuit.

question: The menu says “Soup of the day.” You want to know which soup it is before you order. What do you ask?
choices: Which soup would you recommend?
Could I see the menu again?
How much is the soup, please?
What’s today’s soup, please?
note: The menu only says “Soup of the day.” Asking what today’s soup is gets you the name before you order.

picture.alt: A cooking pot and wooden spoon.

question: You and a friend order tea. She likes hers black and you like a little milk. The waiter asks how to serve it. What do you say?
choices: Could you put a little milk in our tea?
Could you bring us both black tea?
Could we have the milk on the side?
Could we have some sugar with our tea?
note: “Milk in our tea” asks for milk in both cups. “On the side” asks for a separate jug, so each person can choose.

picture.alt: A bowl of white milk pudding.

question: You ordered coffee a moment ago. Now you’d like tea instead. The worker hasn’t made the coffee yet. What do you ask?
choices: Could I have a tea as well?
Could I change my coffee to tea?
Could you make my coffee a little weaker?
Could I have a tea too, please?
note: “Tea too” adds a second drink. “Change my coffee to tea” tells the worker you want just one.

picture.alt: A cup of tea on a saucer with loose tea leaves nearby.

question: You and a friend finish lunch. You each want to pay for exactly what you ordered. What do you ask the waiter?
choices: Could we pay separately, please?
Could I pay for both of us?
Can we pay half each, please?
Could we see the bill first, please?
note: Half each works if you want to share the total equally. Separate bills let you pay for your own orders.

picture.alt: A bottle and a glass of fizzy cola.

question: There are two slices of your pizza left. You enjoyed it and want to eat the rest at home. What do you ask the waiter?
choices: Could I order a whole pizza to take away?
Can I order another one to take home?
Could you leave my plate here a little longer?
Could I take the rest home, please?
note: “Another one” asks for a new pizza. “The rest” means the slices already on your plate.
